facts.label: Financial interpretation
facts.text: Leverage has risen because earnings fell, not because borrowing grew. Reported EBITDA moved from USD 4,573 million in FY2024 to USD 3,395 million in FY2025 and USD 2,916 million over the last twelve months, while total debt moved from USD 25,736 million to USD 25,876 million. Fuel explains most of the recent step: aircraft fuel and related taxes rose by USD 4,427 million, or 55.22%, in the first nine months of 2026, and operating income was USD 535 million against USD 1,042 million a year earlier. facts.label: Financial interpretation
facts.text: Liquidity is the main support for creditors. At September 30, 2026 American reported USD 11,763 million of available liquidity, being cash of USD 1,094 million, short-term investments of USD 7,159 million and undrawn facilities of USD 3,510 million, against USD 4,181 million of principal due before the end of 2027, a cover of 2.81x. The wall is heavier in 2028 at USD 7,861 million, so the test is whether liquidity is preserved or refinancing is available when that year approaches. The filing summarises minimum-liquidity and collateral-value covenants but prints no headroom, and undrawn facilities are committed lines rather than cash, so covenant capacity is not established. facts.label: Financial interpretation
facts.text: Cash generation is flattered by customer-funded balances. Operating cash flow was USD 4,440 million in the first nine months of 2026 against USD 2,229 million a year earlier, and free cash flow after capital expenditures was USD 1,780 million against USD 126 million. Yet customer-funded balances, being the air traffic liability and both loyalty program liabilities, rose by USD 3,206 million to USD 20,928 million since December 31, 2025. These are obligations to provide travel or miles, they follow the season and they are not interest-bearing debt, so the improvement can reverse if bookings slow or redemptions rise; FY2025 free cash flow was USD -1,786 million after capital expenditures of USD 3,716 million. facts.label: Financial interpretation
facts.text: The strongest contrary evidence is the size of liquidity against the principal due before the end of 2027: all of the issuer's debt principal is listed as secured, much of it amortises, maturities run out to 2039, and short-term investments have grown during 2026. That would win if fuel prices fall and quarterly EBITDA recovers toward the FY2025 level, so the observable tests are quarterly operating income, fuel cost, the customer-funded balances and the liquidity figure at the next filing. A downside sequence begins with another fuel price rise or a booking slowdown, first breaks operating cash conversion because customer-funded balances unwind, and then draws on short-term investments to service the 2027 and 2028 principal, which would show as lower liquidity before it shows as a covenant event. rows.label: Chart data: revenue and EBITDA — paragraph 1

limitations: Produced in a host session and accepted by the CP-OS check.
Literal checked analytical handoff, not native contract acceptance; source qualifications and gaps remain.

- Medium: No filing page states the legal rank among the secured instruments, their guarantor or obligor scope beyond the debt note, or covenant headroom, so the ranked debt stack is left empty and secured capacity, recovery and covenant conclusions are not established. Executed agreements and a collateral map would close this. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 61 - Medium: The issuer states no EBITDA or adjusted EBITDA, so reported EBITDA is derived from operating income and depreciation and amortization, no EBITDAR or add-back bridge can be built for the issuer, and the EBITDA bridge is not stated. The parent's adjusted measures belong to a different perimeter. An issuer-level reconciliation would close this. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 201; EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 7 - Medium: Fuel financing of USD 933 million is a secured bank obligation shown outside debt. It is not in total debt, and the amount, repayment schedule and second-priority collateral terms beyond the annual report description are not established. The labelled alternative leverage row shows its effect. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 151 - Low: The nine-month cash flow prints only the operating total, so the nine-month working capital, deferred tax and other operating components, cash taxes paid and capitalised interest are not established for the issuer. Parent commentary attributes higher operating cash flow to the air traffic and loyalty liabilities, but the issuer's own split is not printed. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 61 - Low: Individual instrument carrying values, the dollar amortisation of several term loans, certificate-level schedules and the finance lease terms are not printed; the aggregate reconciliation to total debt is supported, but a complete instrument interest and principal schedule is not. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 220–227 - Low: Repayment terms and security of the receivables from related parties, and the issuer's quarterly cash flow, are not stated, so the amount of cash available to the issuer's own creditors beyond its balance sheet is not established. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 202 - Low: Operating statistics such as capacity, load factor and yield are printed for the parent including regional carriers, not for the issuer, so no issuer-level operating series is shown, and nothing dated after October 22, 2026 was supplied, so events to the cutoff are not established. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 48; Source readiness (CP-0)

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The issuer's cash is moving to its parent as loans, not dividends. The net receivable from the parent was USD 12,512 million at September 30, 2026 against USD 11,938 million at year-end, and the annual report says part of the earlier increase was American funding the parent's USD 1.0 billion cash settlement of its convertible notes in July 2025. Cash lent this way is no longer available to repay American's own debt until the parent repays it, so the parent's liquidity and refinancing ability matter to the issuer's creditors; repayment terms are not stated. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 40–41; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 257; calculation C05

facts.text: Financing in 2026 was creditor-neutral to constructive, but it added secured debt. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against concern is that lending to the parent is intragroup, the parent guarantees much of the issuer's debt, and the issuer reports USD 11,763 million of available liquidity with no dividend leakage. If the parent repays the receivable or discloses that it is repayable on demand, the governance risk would fall to low; if the receivable keeps growing while earnings weaken, or the parent funds distributions, buybacks or its own long-dated debt maturities from American's cash, the risk would rise to high. facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Ranked weaknesses. First, high leverage driven by fuel: reported EBITDA of USD 2,916 million over the last twelve months against debt of USD 25,876 million gives 8.87x, and unhedged fuel passes price shocks directly to earnings, which leaves little capacity to absorb another shock. Fourth, debt that is entirely secured, with 55.75% linked to aircraft and engines, so more borrowing adds claims on the same collateral. Fifth, a net receivable from the parent of USD 12,512 million, which makes the issuer's cash partly dependent on the parent's credit. facts.label: Industry forces and framework read
facts.text: Competition is intense and the filings list competitive, regulatory, labour and fuel risks as the main pressures; the credit translation is that sector pricing and cost shocks reach earnings faster than debt can be reduced. Regulatory and policy factors matter through antitrust litigation at the parent group and aviation regulation, and macroeconomic demand matters through leisure and corporate travel; none of these has a quantified effect in the sources. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The supported downside begins with fuel staying near the parent's assumed level or rising, or with a booking slowdown. Revenue growth then fails to cover fuel, and because labour is contracted and fuel is unhedged, EBITDA falls below the USD 2,916 million last-twelve-month level and cover below 2.06x. Free cash flow turns negative as customer-funded balances stop rising, drawing on the USD 7,159 million of short-term investments, while aircraft commitments continue. Liquidity of USD 11,763 million is enough to avoid distress through 2027, but it only equals the principal due through 2028, so the first financial break would be refinancing of the 2028 maturities on secured terms against aircraft and loyalty collateral. ## Findings
### Bottom line

Total debt reached 8.87x last-twelve-month reported EBITDA at September 30, 2026, up from 5.63x at the end of 2024, so creditors of American Airlines, Inc. depend on USD 11,763 million of available liquidity and collateral rather than earnings cover.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; calculation C03; calculation C05; calculation C09

The fall in earnings is led by fuel: aircraft fuel and related taxes rose by USD 4,427 million in the first nine months of 2026 while revenue grew 15.63%. Debt rose only USD 617 million since December 31, 2025, and liquidity covers the USD 4,181 million of principal due before the end of 2027 by 2.81x, while interest paid over the last twelve months is covered 2.06x.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 66; calculation C09; calculation C11; calculation C12

### Financial interpretation

Leverage has risen because earnings fell, not because borrowing grew. Reported EBITDA moved from USD 4,573 million in FY2024 to USD 3,395 million in FY2025 and USD 2,916 million over the last twelve months, while total debt moved from USD 25,736 million to USD 25,876 million. Fuel explains most of the recent step: aircraft fuel and related taxes rose by USD 4,427 million, or 55.22%, in the first nine months of 2026, and operating income was USD 535 million against USD 1,042 million a year earlier. The nine-month EBITDA margin fell to 4.21% from 6.05%, so the fuel price path is the main swing factor for leverage: lower prices would help and higher prices would extend the deterioration.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 58; calculation C02; calculation C03; calculation C11; calculation C15

Interest cover has slipped more gently than leverage, from 2.53x in FY2024 to 2.19x in FY2025 and 2.06x over the last twelve months, because interest paid fell from USD 1,806 million in FY2024 to USD 1,551 million in FY2025 and USD 1,416 million over the last twelve months as the issuer repaid higher-cost debt. That offset is finite: cover on reported EBITDA is thin for a business whose fixed charges also include aircraft rent and large purchase commitments, and interest paid is not a fixed-charge measure.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 254; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 27; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 59; calculation C05

Liquidity is the main support for creditors. At September 30, 2026 American reported USD 11,763 million of available liquidity, being cash of USD 1,094 million, short-term investments of USD 7,159 million and undrawn facilities of USD 3,510 million, against USD 4,181 million of principal due before the end of 2027, a cover of 2.81x. The wall is heavier in 2028 at USD 7,861 million, so the test is whether liquidity is preserved or refinancing is available when that year approaches. The filing summarises minimum-liquidity and collateral-value covenants but prints no headroom, and undrawn facilities are committed lines rather than cash, so covenant capacity is not established.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 66; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 59–61; calculation C08; calculation C09

Cash generation is flattered by customer-funded balances. Operating cash flow was USD 4,440 million in the first nine months of 2026 against USD 2,229 million a year earlier, and free cash flow after capital expenditures was USD 1,780 million against USD 126 million. Yet customer-funded balances, being the air traffic liability and both loyalty program liabilities, rose by USD 3,206 million to USD 20,928 million since December 31, 2025. These are obligations to provide travel or miles, they follow the season and they are not interest-bearing debt, so the improvement can reverse if bookings slow or redemptions rise; FY2025 free cash flow was USD -1,786 million after capital expenditures of USD 3,716 million.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 201–202; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 26–27; calculation C10; calculation C13

The issuer also lends to its affiliates. Receivables from related parties were USD 10,430 million at September 30, 2026, USD 534 million higher than at year-end, and the 2025 cash flow shows a USD 1,701 million outflow for this line inside operating activities. Repayment terms are not established from the statements, so these balances support group liquidity but their availability to the issuer's own creditors is not shown. Parent debt of USD 29,635 million exceeds the issuer's USD 25,876 million by USD 3,759 million, so the parent's net debt target, which also counts leases and pensions, is on a wider definition than any ratio here.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 202; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 6; calculation C14; calculation C16

Fuel financing of USD 933 million is, as the annual report describes it, a bank facility at one-month SOFR plus 3.75%, secured on a second-priority basis by brand intellectual property, and the issuer shows it on its own line outside debt. Counting it lifts total debt to 9.19x last-twelve-month EBITDA, so the fixed ratios understate claims on the issuer's assets and the labelled alternative should be read beside them.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 151; calculation C06

No event after September 30, 2026 with a stated effect on net debt was found. In October 2026 American exercised purchase options for five Airbus A320 Family aircraft and committed to purchase two Boeing 777-200ER aircraft in the fourth quarter; no price or financing is stated for them individually, so they stay out of period figures.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 65

The strongest contrary evidence is the size of liquidity against the principal due before the end of 2027: all of the issuer's debt principal is listed as secured, much of it amortises, maturities run out to 2039, and short-term investments have grown during 2026. That would win if fuel prices fall and quarterly EBITDA recovers toward the FY2025 level, so the observable tests are quarterly operating income, fuel cost, the customer-funded balances and the liquidity figure at the next filing. A downside sequence begins with another fuel price rise or a booking slowdown, first breaks operating cash conversion because customer-funded balances unwind, and then draws on short-term investments to service the 2027 and 2028 principal, which would show as lower liquidity before it shows as a covenant event.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 66; EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 6

## Gaps

- Medium: No filing page states the legal rank among the secured instruments, their guarantor or obligor scope beyond the debt note, or covenant headroom, so the ranked debt stack is left empty and secured capacity, recovery and covenant conclusions are not established. Executed agreements and a collateral map would close this.

- Medium: The issuer states no EBITDA or adjusted EBITDA, so reported EBITDA is derived from operating income and depreciation and amortization, no EBITDAR or add-back bridge can be built for the issuer, and the EBITDA bridge is not stated. The parent's adjusted measures belong to a different perimeter. An issuer-level reconciliation would close this.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 201; EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 7

- Medium: Fuel financing of USD 933 million is a secured bank obligation shown outside debt. It is not in total debt, and the amount, repayment schedule and second-priority collateral terms beyond the annual report description are not established. The labelled alternative leverage row shows its effect.

- Low: The nine-month cash flow prints only the operating total, so the nine-month working capital, deferred tax and other operating components, cash taxes paid and capitalised interest are not established for the issuer. Parent commentary attributes higher operating cash flow to the air traffic and loyalty liabilities, but the issuer's own split is not printed.

- Low: Individual instrument carrying values, the dollar amortisation of several term loans, certificate-level schedules and the finance lease terms are not printed; the aggregate reconciliation to total debt is supported, but a complete instrument interest and principal schedule is not.

- Low: Repayment terms and security of the receivables from related parties, and the issuer's quarterly cash flow, are not stated, so the amount of cash available to the issuer's own creditors beyond its balance sheet is not established.

- Low: Operating statistics such as capacity, load factor and yield are printed for the parent including regional carriers, not for the issuer, so no issuer-level operating series is shown, and nothing dated after October 22, 2026 was supplied, so events to the cutoff are not established.

## Request

The scope is the issuer's own business and its relationship with its parent, using the annual report for 2025 and the third-quarter 2026 report.

## Findings
### Bottom line

American is wholly owned by its parent with no sponsor, and creditors' main governance risk is cash lent upstream to the parent rather than retained: the net receivable from the parent reached USD 12,512 million.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 40–41; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 9; calculation C05

The parent otherwise looks supportive: it guarantees the issuer's credit facilities and the AAdvantage financing, the issuer's equity statement shows no dividend, and 2026 financing refinanced and extended debt rather than restructuring it. Governance detail for the issuer itself is omitted from the annual report, so board control and related-party terms are not established.
### Key findings

The issuer's cash is moving to its parent as loans, not dividends. The net receivable from the parent was USD 12,512 million at September 30, 2026 against USD 11,938 million at year-end, and the annual report says part of the earlier increase was American funding the parent's USD 1.0 billion cash settlement of its convertible notes in July 2025. Cash lent this way is no longer available to repay American's own debt until the parent repays it, so the parent's liquidity and refinancing ability matter to the issuer's creditors; repayment terms are not stated.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 40–41; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 257; calculation C05

The parent supports the issuer's debt rather than extracting from it. It guarantees American's credit facilities as a senior unsecured obligation, guarantees the AAdvantage notes and term loans together with special-purpose guarantors, and has in certain cases guaranteed equipment notes, while the issuer's equity statement shows no dividend paid and the parent paid no cash dividend or share repurchase in 2025 or 2024. The guarantees are only as strong as the parent's own balance sheet, which carries separate debt outside the issuer.

The loyalty program gives the business an unusually durable cash source. Loyalty revenue was 13.42% of operating revenues in the first nine months of 2026, and the group received USD 6.2 billion of cash from co-branded card and other partners in 2025, but the same program carries the largest customer-funded liability and also backs the AAdvantage secured financing, so a weaker partner relationship would hit liquidity and collateral together.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 29; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 167–168; calculation C02

Cost flexibility is limited and fuel is unhedged. Salaries, wages and benefits were 30.18% of operating expenses in the first nine months of 2026, about 86% of the group's employees are covered by labour contracts, and the group had no fuel hedges outstanding at the end of 2025 under a policy not to hedge. Margins therefore move with fuel prices and wage settlements and not with management cost actions.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 110; calculation C07

Financing in 2026 was creditor-neutral to constructive, but it added secured debt. American extended its revolving facilities to 2031, refinanced and upsized its 2014 term loan to a 2033 maturity, repaid its short-term term loan, prepaid the 8.50% senior secured notes and issued three new aircraft and engine pass-through certificate series plus equipment loans. Cash-flow proceeds exceeded payments by USD 590 million for the nine months even after retirements of USD 1,939 million, so the effect is a longer, more secured maturity profile and not a smaller debt stock.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 32–36; calculation C06

Governance transparency for the issuer is thin. American omits the executive, director and ownership items of its annual report under the reduced-disclosure rules, the parent's proxy statement was not supplied, and the audit opinion and controls conclusions are clean, so the weakness is missing detail, not adverse findings. The parent's tax benefit preservation plan, which runs to October 2027, deters certain share acquisitions and so lowers the chance of a tax-driven ownership change during that period.
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against concern is that lending to the parent is intragroup, the parent guarantees much of the issuer's debt, and the issuer reports USD 11,763 million of available liquidity with no dividend leakage. If the parent repays the receivable or discloses that it is repayable on demand, the governance risk would fall to low; if the receivable keeps growing while earnings weaken, or the parent funds distributions, buybacks or its own long-dated debt maturities from American's cash, the risk would rise to high.
### Limitations
- The repayment terms and security of the receivable from the parent are not stated, so the finding that cash is trapped upstream may overstate the risk if the balance is repayable on demand.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 40–41
- Board, control, fee and sponsor-style disclosure for the issuer is omitted, so the medium governance risk level rests on observed behaviour, not on control rights.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 3

- No executed agreements were supplied, so the finding that 2026 financing was creditor-neutral rests on the filings' descriptions of terms, and guarantee scope beyond those descriptions is not established.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 164–168; Source readiness (CP-0)
- Nothing dated after October 22, 2026 was supplied, so later financing, distributions or litigation outcomes could change the behaviour findings.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0)

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

No acquisition, sponsor transaction or change of control is stated for the issuer, so the summary is of its 2026 debt activity. In February 2026 the 2025 AAdvantage term loan was amended to lower its margin, and in March 2026 the three revolving facilities were re-established with commitments to March 2031. In May 2026 the 2014 term loan was refinanced and increased to a May 2033 maturity, and aircraft and engine financing continued through three pass-through certificate programs in May, June and August 2026 and USD 705 million of new equipment loans.

The issuer also retired debt: the short-term term loan, which was due in January 2026, was repaid in full, the 8.50% senior secured notes were prepaid in full, and USD 310 million of equipment notes under earlier pass-through certificates was prepaid. Of the August 2026 certificates, about USD 633 million of proceeds was still held in escrow at September 30, 2026 and is not reported as debt until further equipment notes are issued, so reported debt excludes that amount for now.

## Request

Fundamental credit synthesis for AMERICAN AIRLINES, INC. (american-airlines-inc), as of 2026-11-05, under the credit_snapshot pathway. The scope is the issuer's business, financial profile, downside path and monitoring triggers, built from the supplied analyses and the issuer's filings.

## Findings
### Bottom line

American's fundamental credit profile is adequate but strained: a large hub-and-loyalty business and USD 11,763 million of liquidity support creditors, while fuel-driven earnings pressure has lifted total debt to 8.87x last-twelve-month reported EBITDA and left interest cover at 2.06x.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C01; calculation C03

The primary downside path is another fuel spike or demand slowdown that cuts EBITDA while customer-funded cash unwinds, drawing on liquidity that covers principal due through 2028 only 0.98x. Refinancing capacity rests on aircraft collateral and loyalty assets, and the parent relationship adds support through guarantees and risk through USD 12,512 million of cash lent upstream.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C03; calculation C07
### Key findings

- Leverage is high because earnings fell, not because debt grew. Reported EBITDA fell from USD 4,573 million in FY2024 to USD 2,916 million over the last twelve months while debt stayed near USD 25,876 million, taking total debt to 8.87x; unhedged fuel and contract-bound labour costs pass price shocks straight into EBITDA, so creditors carry fuel risk without a cushion.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C04

- Interest cover is thin. Interest paid took 48.56% of last-twelve-month EBITDA, so cover of 2.06x leaves little room before cash interest competes with maturities and aircraft deliveries for liquidity.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C02

- Liquidity is the main protection but is finite. USD 11,763 million of available liquidity covers the USD 4,181 million of principal due before the end of 2027 by 2.81x, yet it only matches the USD 12,042 million due through 2028, so access to refinancing, not cash on hand, decides the 2028 outcome.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C03

- Recent cash flow is flattered by customer-funded balances. Free cash flow of USD 1,780 million in the first nine months of 2026 came with a USD 3,206 million rise in air traffic and loyalty liabilities, which unwind if bookings slow.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C05; calculation C06

- Support from the parent is real but runs both ways. The parent guarantees the issuer's credit facilities and the AAdvantage financing and no dividend is evidenced, yet the issuer has lent USD 12,512 million net to the parent, so the issuer's liquidity is partly a claim on the parent group.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C07
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case that the view is too cautious is that last-twelve-month EBITDA is depressed by a fuel spike: fuel cost rose 55.22% in nine months while revenue grew 15.63%, the parent guides to continued growth in fourth-quarter revenue, and 2026 financing pushed the revolving facilities to 2031 and a term loan to 2033. A fall in fuel prices that restores EBITDA toward the FY2025 level would cut leverage from 8.87x toward 7.44x without any debt reduction. The view would turn more negative if liquidity fell below the principal due before the end of 2027, if the receivable from the parent grew while earnings weakened, or if refinancing of the 2028 maturities needed additional collateral beyond aircraft.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 6; calculation C01; calculation C03; calculation C04; calculation C11
### Limitations

- Leverage is measured on reported EBITDA after aircraft rent, on debt that excludes operating lease liabilities, and over a single trailing window, so the finding that leverage is high and cover thin could look different on a lease-adjusted or fuel-normalised basis that this analysis does not build.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1)
- No peer or sector benchmark was run, so the adequate rating of the business profile is relative to the issuer's own history and sources, not to other airlines.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0)
- The outlook rests on parent-level management guidance for the fourth quarter and full year, so the direction of earnings is indicative and carries no issuer-level forecast.
Basis: EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 6
- Covenant headroom and executed financing terms are not available, so the view that liquidity protects creditors excludes any minimum-liquidity covenant that could restrict use of cash.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 61; Source readiness (CP-0)
### Strengths and weaknesses

Ranked weaknesses. First, high leverage driven by fuel: reported EBITDA of USD 2,916 million over the last twelve months against debt of USD 25,876 million gives 8.87x, and unhedged fuel passes price shocks directly to earnings, which leaves little capacity to absorb another shock. Second, thin cover of 2.06x with interest paid at 48.56% of EBITDA, which raises the cost of any shortfall. Third, a 2028 maturity of USD 7,861 million that exceeds what liquidity covers alone. Fourth, debt that is entirely secured, with 55.75% linked to aircraft and engines, so more borrowing adds claims on the same collateral. Fifth, a net receivable from the parent of USD 12,512 million, which makes the issuer's cash partly dependent on the parent's credit.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C03; calculation C07; calculation C09

Ranked strengths. First, liquidity of USD 11,763 million including USD 7,159 million of short-term investments, which covers principal due before the end of 2027 by 2.81x. Second, a network and loyalty business in which loyalty revenue was 13.42% of revenue and partners paid USD 6.2 billion of cash to the group in 2025, a recurring source that supports financing against loyalty assets. Third, demonstrated refinancing access in 2026, when revolvers were extended to 2031, a term loan to 2033 and three aircraft certificate programs were placed. Fourth, a parent that guarantees key debt and paid no dividend.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C03; calculation C08

### Business profile and ownership

American is a network carrier that sells scheduled passenger and cargo service through nine hubs, with regional carriers flying under capacity purchase agreements, and it is wholly owned by its parent. Domestic routes were 70.89% of passenger revenue in the first nine months of 2026 and loyalty revenue 13.42% of operating revenues, so the business draws on passenger demand across its network and on a loyalty program whose partner cash and mileage balances act as recurring funding. No customer concentration is stated. The group structure matters for creditors: the parent guarantees American's credit facilities and the AAdvantage financing, but it carries its own debt and has received USD 12,512 million of net cash from the issuer, so the issuer is both supported by and a funder of the group.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C07; calculation C08
### Revenue, costs and cash conversion

Revenue is cyclical and partly discretionary but backed by loyalty income: revenue grew 15.63% in the nine months to September 30, 2026, so demand has held, yet pricing power did not offset fuel, whose cost rose 55.22%. Costs are largely fixed in the short run because about 86% of the group's employees are covered by labour contracts and fuel is unhedged by policy, which means margins shrink first when fuel rises, and creditors rather than management cost actions carry the gap. Capital intensity is high, with USD 24,056 million of aircraft and engine commitments against nine-month capital expenditures of USD 2,660 million, and free cash flow of USD 1,780 million in the nine months was helped by a USD 3,206 million rise in customer-funded balances, so durable conversion of EBITDA to debt service cash is not yet shown.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 110; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 65–66; calculation C04; calculation C05; calculation C06; calculation C10
### Industry forces and framework read

Competition is intense and the filings list competitive, regulatory, labour and fuel risks as the main pressures; the credit translation is that sector pricing and cost shocks reach earnings faster than debt can be reduced. Rivalry and fuel are the forces that move margins, while supplier concentration in aircraft and engines delays deliveries and raises financing needs. Regulatory and policy factors matter through antitrust litigation at the parent group and aviation regulation, and macroeconomic demand matters through leisure and corporate travel; none of these has a quantified effect in the sources. In credit terms the supportive items are network scale, loyalty cash and a parent that guarantees debt, and the constraining items are leverage, fuel exposure and secured-debt concentration.
### Financial profile and credit quality

Scale and market position are adequate: the network is broad but no market share is stated. Competitive advantage rests on the loyalty program and hubs and is adequate. Business diversification is weak to adequate, with 70.89% of passenger revenue domestic and no customer data. Cost and capex flexibility are weak, because labour is contracted, fuel is unhedged and commitments are large. Margin stability is weak: the EBITDA margin on the nine months fell with fuel. Free cash flow stability is weak to adequate because recent strength depends on customer-funded balances. Ability to refinance is adequate, evidenced by 2026 transactions but limited by secured-only debt and the group's non-investment-grade corporate credit rating. Liquidity is adequate for the next five quarters and only matches principal through 2028. Financial policy and governance are adequate: no dividend and parent guarantees, offset by cash lent to the parent. The trend is down on leverage and cover and flat on liquidity, and the missing data are executed agreements, covenant headroom and the terms of the receivable from the parent.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 33; calculation C01; calculation C03; calculation C07; calculation C08
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over twelve to twenty-four months the parent guides to fourth-quarter revenue growth of 19.5% to 22.5% and a full-year 2026 adjusted loss per share of USD (1.60) to USD (1.00), on an assumed fuel price of about USD 4.70 per gallon, so earnings stay under pressure through year-end and leverage on trailing EBITDA is unlikely to improve before 2027. Tailwinds are revenue growth, loyalty cash, extended maturities and loyalty cash; headwinds are fuel, contract wage increases and the USD 7,861 million 2028 maturity. Over three to five years the question is whether fleet renewal funded by secured debt lifts margins enough to reduce leverage; the sources give no issuer-level forecast, so that is not established.
Basis: EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 6; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C03; calculation C11
### Downside scenario

The supported downside begins with fuel staying near the parent's assumed level or rising, or with a booking slowdown. Revenue growth then fails to cover fuel, and because labour is contracted and fuel is unhedged, EBITDA falls below the USD 2,916 million last-twelve-month level and cover below 2.06x. Free cash flow turns negative as customer-funded balances stop rising, drawing on the USD 7,159 million of short-term investments, while aircraft commitments continue. Liquidity of USD 11,763 million is enough to avoid distress through 2027, but it only equals the principal due through 2028, so the first financial break would be refinancing of the 2028 maturities on secured terms against aircraft and loyalty collateral. Possible management levers are drawing the undrawn facilities and slowing lending to the parent, while deferral of aircraft deliveries is not established by the sources; resilience looks sufficient to avoid a liquidity crisis in 2027 and uncertain for 2028. No numerical stress result is established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C02; calculation C03; calculation C05
### Overall credit view

Overall, American presents an adequate business profile supported by a broad network, loyalty cash and liquidity, but credit quality is constrained by leverage of 8.87x reported EBITDA, thin cover of 2.06x and unhedged fuel exposure. Cash-flow durability appears adequate but flattered by customer-funded balances. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on aircraft and loyalty collateral, market access for secured debt and the parent's credit, since the parent guarantees key debt and holds USD 12,512 million of the issuer's cash. The primary downside path is fuel-driven earnings compression that consumes liquidity before the 2028 maturities. Further analysis would require executed agreements, covenant headroom, the terms of the parent receivable and an issuer-level outlook. Top risk: fuel-driven earnings compression.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C01; calculation C03; calculation C07
